outputs.L1:
No chain-link fences leapt in a single bound. No juke-move Nike commercial; no speeding-bullet, Skittles-hued cross-trainers. No grand jeté over the little blue recycling bin, a prism of clouds rising beneath his feet.

No body all-fucked in boot cuffs wide enough to cloak court-appointed tethers. Or slumped over, hoodie-shrouded—“sheepishly scary,” according to one eyewitness. Definitely not your Louis V. sweatsuit red-carpet fashion review, coming to you live from E! and Fox News outside the morgue.

No chance for homeboy in the peekaboo boxer shorts. Homeboy with the frozen wrists. Iced. Homeslice with the paisley Pretty Flacko flag flying by the seat of low-slung denim—no defense attorney gets to call me Gang Related. Tupac in a mock-leather bomber.

No statement taken from the Clint Eastwood of your particular planned community, saying he had the right to stand his ground at the Super Target because my flat-billed, fitted cap cast a shady shadow over his shoulder in the checkout line.

No, siree.

See, I practice self-target practice. There is no sight of me in my wears. I’m bedecked in No-Wrinkle Dockers. Sensible navy blazer. Barack Obama tie, Double-Consciousness-knotted. Stock dandelion pinned to the skin of an American lapel, with his head blown off.
outputs.L2:
There were no chain-link fences cleared in one miraculous jump. No Nike-ad sidestep, no Skittles-colored cross-trainers moving faster than gunfire. No dark-skinned Adonis winding through cobblestone streets, leaving ribbons of industrial Vaseline behind him. No Heisman feint around garbage cans. No grand jeté over the small blue recycling bin with a rainbow of clouds blooming underfoot.

No one, completely fucked, wore boot cuffs broad enough to conceal court-ordered monitors. No one sagged beneath a hood, looking—according to one witness—both timid and frightening. This certainly would not become a Louis Vuitton sweatsuit fashion critique, broadcast live by E! and Fox News from outside the morgue.

The brother in the boxers showing above his waistband never got a chance. His wrists were stopped cold. Frozen. The paisley banner of Pretty Flacko flew from the rear of his low-hanging jeans—but no defense lawyer will be allowed to label me gang-affiliated. Picture Tupac in a fake-leather bomber jacket.

No statement came from the Clint Eastwood figure of your master-planned neighborhood, insisting that he was entitled to stand his ground inside Super Target because my fitted, flat-brimmed cap threw a suspicious shadow across his shoulder in the checkout line. No, sir.

You see, I conduct target practice on myself. Nothing I wear makes me visible. I am dressed in wrinkle-resistant Dockers, a practical navy blazer, and a Barack Obama tie knotted in Double Consciousness. A standard-issue dandelion is fastened to the flesh of an American lapel, its head blasted away.
outputs.L3:
The speaker rejects the stereotypical images through which Black men are often portrayed in the media: running as if fleeing a crime, displaying extraordinary athletic ability for public entertainment, or appearing inherently dangerous. These narrow representations reduce Black masculinity to criminality, physical performance, or threat, denying Black men their individuality and humanity.

Clothing plays a central role in this stereotyping. Hoodies, sagging jeans, fitted caps, and visible boxer shorts are treated not simply as fashion choices but as supposed evidence of gang affiliation or criminal intent. The text exposes how racial prejudice transforms ordinary clothing into a justification for suspicion, surveillance, and violence. A Black man may be judged as dangerous before he speaks or acts, based only on his appearance.

The speaker also criticizes the broader systems that enable such judgments, including racial profiling, “stand your ground” laws, and media coverage that dehumanizes Black victims. These forces often shift blame away from those who commit violence and onto the people who suffer it. By emphasizing a victim’s clothing, behavior, or background, media narratives can imply that the victim caused or deserved the violence inflicted upon him.

In response, the speaker adopts conservative, conventionally respectable clothing as a strategy of self-protection. Dressing carefully becomes a kind of camouflage intended to help him blend into mainstream American society and avoid being perceived as a threat. This choice is not presented as simple personal preference; rather, it reflects the exhausting pressure placed on Black Americans to manage other people’s prejudice in order to remain safe.

Yet the final image undermines any confidence that respectability or assimilation can provide complete protection. Even when a Black person follows social expectations, dresses conservatively, and attempts to appear nonthreatening, racial violence may still find him. The conclusion therefore exposes the limits of respectability politics: changing one’s appearance cannot eliminate systemic racism, nor can conformity guarantee safety in a society that continues to view Blackness itself as threatening.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts racial profiling and anti-Black violence by exposing the stereotypes through which Black people are so often viewed. Rather than presenting the speaker as threatening, rebellious, or sensationalized, it emphasizes his deliberately respectable and assimilated appearance. His carefully chosen clothing becomes a form of self-protection: by dressing according to dominant social expectations, he attempts to make himself legible as harmless, disciplined, and worthy of respect. This contrast reveals the cruel logic of respectability politics, which pressures marginalized people to suppress signs of difference in the hope that conformity will shield them from suspicion and violence.

Yet the poem ultimately shows that such efforts cannot overcome the racism imposed on the speaker from outside. No degree of restraint, refinement, or self-erasure can prevent a racist society from projecting danger onto a Black body. The final image is especially devastating because it collapses the supposed distinction between the “respectable” individual and the racial stereotype: despite everything the speaker has done to appear safe, he remains vulnerable to being misread, targeted, and killed. In this way, the poem rejects the idea that victims of racial violence could have protected themselves by behaving or dressing differently. Its conclusion underscores the lethal persistence of racism in American life, revealing that the problem lies not in the speaker’s appearance or conduct but in a culture that continues to treat Blackness itself as a threat.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem about a Black man imagining how respectability politics cannot protect him from racial profiling and gun violence in America.
counterfactuals.output: He irons his name until it lies flat as a white flag. He buttons his vowels, knots his degrees around his throat, keeps both hands at ten and two as if steering the moon through a neighborhood of wolves. Yes, sir. No, sir. Wallet in the glove box, registration bright as a hymn. Still the red light blooms behind him—an artificial sunset—and every lesson his mother folded into his body begins to tremble: don’t reach, don’t run, don’t become sudden weather. He imagines respectability as a glass umbrella in a country raining bullets, beautiful, useless, already cracked. His suit cannot testify before the gun. His polished shoes cannot outrun suspicion. The officer approaches wearing the whole night on his belt, and the man sees himself multiplied in the mirror: graduate, father, neighbor, threat; each version holding an invisible weapon carved from somebody else’s fear. Somewhere a television rehearses his obituary, selecting the least forgiving photograph. Somewhere a jury sleeps inside a locked door. He lowers the window and America leans in, smelling for guilt. He has made himself small enough to fit inside every command, yet the commands keep shrinking. He imagines his skin as a dark star the nation mistakes for a target; imagines the Constitution as a paper shield dissolving on his tongue. Then the flashlight enters him, cold and official, searching his ribs for a reason. He breathes carefully. Even breath can be misconstrued. Above them, the moon raises its pale hands and is believed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental spoken-word monologue that satirizes media coverage of a young Black shooting victim, using sports imagery, brand names, fragmented syntax, and dark humor.
counterfactuals.output:
**INSTANT REPLAY**

Tonight’s top story—  
a boy has been converted  
into footage.

Please stand by  
while our panel of experts  
measures his childhood  
in slow motion.

Nike on his feet.  
Skittles in his pocket.  
A future—unconfirmed brand.

The commentators lean forward:

*Was he fast?*  
*Was he respectful?*  
*Did he make the correct split-second decision*  
*not to be mistaken for a threat?*

Let’s go to the telestrator.

Here—  
the yellow circle around his body.

Here—  
the arrow pointing toward Suspicion.

Here—  
the dotted route he should have run  
to escape the defender,  
the neighborhood,  
the national imagination.

A remarkable failure of footwork.

Back after this message  
from Allstate.

Are you in good hands?

The boy is unavailable for comment.  
His mother is available  
but only in a small box  
beside an advertisement  
for a Ford F-150:

**BUILT TOUGH.**

She is not allowed to be tough.  
Too angry.

Not allowed to collapse.  
Too theatrical.

Please grieve  
in a manner suitable  
for syndication.

At halftime,  
they examine his stats:

Age: young enough for tragedy.  
Height: tall enough for menace.  
Grade-point average: suddenly relevant.  
Photograph: smiling—biased.  
Photograph: unsmiling—evidence.

The anchor says  
“allegedly”  
like a mouthguard.

The anchor says  
“urban”  
and the studio lights nod.

The anchor says  
“we may never know”  
while everyone already knows  
which version sells.

Tonight’s MVP:  
the passive voice.

Shots were fired.  
A life was lost.  
Questions remain.

No one did anything.  
Grammar pulled the trigger  
and fled the scene.

Now a word from Coca-Cola:

Open happiness.

The scoreboard reads:

Home: one funeral.  
Away: one paid suspension.  
America: leading the series  
four hundred years to zero.

But wait—  
official review.

Was the boy perfect?

Did he volunteer on weekends?  
Rescue kittens?  
Play violin for veterans  
while maintaining eye contact  
with authority?

No?

Then the ruling stands.

The crowd goes mild.

ESPN has his wingspan.  
CNN has his worst selfie.  
Fox has a question mark  
wearing a police badge.  
TikTok has a dance  
before the coffin closes.

And somewhere,  
a producer whispers:

Can we get rain at the vigil?  
Rain performs well.

Can we get candles?  
Candles say *healing*  
without demanding anything.

Can we get the mother  
to say forgiveness  
before the next commercial break?

Time is money.  
Dead air is expensive.  
Dead boys—

well.

Tonight, his name scrolls beneath  
weather, stocks,  
and a limited-time offer  
from Amazon Prime.

Tomorrow, another draft pick.

Another body called “incident.”  
Another childhood called “complicated.”  
Another nation calling timeout  
after the buzzer,

asking whether justice  
had possession.

The camera pulls back.

The arena is empty.

The sponsors remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a politically charged prose poem in which the speaker rejects stereotypes associated with hoodies, sagging jeans, and gang affiliation, then adopts business attire only to remain a target.
counterfactuals.output:
They said the hoodie made me suspicious, so I folded it into a dark square and buried it beneath the bed. They said my jeans sagged like a confession, that every inch below the waist was evidence, so I bought a belt and cinched myself upright. They said my friends were a gang because we stood together, laughing too loudly beneath a streetlamp, because brotherhood in our mouths sounded like conspiracy in theirs. I walked away alone.

I cut my hair. Lowered my voice. Learned the clean grammar of handshakes. I buttoned myself into a navy suit, knotted respectability at my throat, polished my shoes until the city flashed in them. I carried a briefcase instead of fear, though fear fit inside. I climbed glass buildings, spoke in charts, arrived early, stayed late, made profit for men who called me articulate as if surprised I had survived my own tongue.

Still, the guard followed me through the lobby. Still, the elevator fell silent when I entered. Still, blue lights rehearsed my funeral in the rearview mirror. *License. Registration. Step out, sir.* The suit did not raise its hands fast enough. The tie could not testify. My résumé lay facedown on the asphalt while a knee translated my pulse into probable cause.

So tell me again about the hoodie. Tell me fabric is the danger, posture the crime, friendship the gang. I changed the costume and kept the sentence. I became the photograph they demanded and remained the target they required.

Now I wear whatever I please. Not because cloth is armor, but because I am done tailoring my body to fit the narrow mercy of your gaze.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a nonlinear poem exploring double consciousness, “stand your ground” culture, and the performance of respectable Black masculinity, ending with a disturbing patriotic image.
counterfactuals.output:
**Dress Code for the Crosshairs**

Before I leave the house,  
my mother irons my name flat.

No wrinkles, she says.  
No sudden reaching.  
No bass loud enough to become a motive.

In the mirror, two men rehearse me:

one knots the tie  
until his throat learns obedience;

one watches the window  
for a country approaching  
with its hand already inside its coat.

*

The ground is always standing.  
It has lawyers.  
It has a porch light, a neighborhood app,  
a mouth full of property lines.

I am told to stand mine  
without appearing to stand.

So I practice stillness—  
that old Black magic  
of becoming harmless  
while being harmed.

Yes, sir.  
No, officer.  
My wallet is—  
May I—  
I have a degree—  
I live right over—

Somewhere, a trigger  
completes my sentence.

*

Tomorrow comes first:

my son asks why the flag  
has so many stripes  
and I say because a nation, too,  
must learn to dress thin wounds  
as decoration.

Yesterday comes after:

a boy in a hoodie  
walks home carrying sweetness.  
Rain beads on his shoulders.  
A stranger names the weather  
suspicion.

Between them, I polish my shoes  
until they shine like evidence.

*

At work I lower my voice  
into the acceptable register,  
trim thunder from each syllable,  
keep my hands where history  
can see them.

The meeting smiles.

The meeting says articulate.

The meeting says intimidating  
in an email marked confidential.

I bring potato salad to the picnic,  
laugh small,  
discuss interest rates,  
grill meat I am careful not to call burnt.

My colleagues say,  
You’re one of the good ones,

and somewhere inside my jacket  
the other me is pounding  
on the glass.

*

Who gets to be a man  
without becoming a threat?

Who gets anger  
without a body count?

I have worn respectability  
like a white glove  
to lift the hot pan of citizenship.

Still, the smoke alarm  
knows my face.

Still, the ground claims fear.

Still, fear receives a badge,  
a camera angle,  
a jury of its reflections.

*

My father taught me:

Carry yourself tall.

My country taught me:

Not that tall.

My father taught me:

Look a man in the eye.

My country:

Not for too long.

My father:

Protect your family.

My country:

From whom?

The answer enters backward,  
already acquitted.

*

Tonight I undress in the dark.

Tie.  
Belt.  
Smile.  
Diploma.  
Receipt.  
Hands.

I place them neatly  
beside the bed  
in case the morning asks  
what I was doing here.

Outside, sprinklers click  
like safeties released.

A lawn sign says  
GOD BLESS.

A siren harmonizes.

And at dawn, the flag rises over the courthouse—  
red stripes wet and widening,  
white stripes pulled tight as a sheet,  
fifty stars pinned over a Black man’s open eyes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a breathless, image-heavy piece of literary poetry about racial surveillance and self-erasure, juxtaposing Nike, Skittles, Fox News, Tupac, Obama-era symbolism, and suburban consumer spaces.
counterfactuals.output:
In the blue-light chapel of Walmart  
the cameras bloom like iron moons,  
each aisle a runway, each black body  
asked to become receipt, barcode, apology—

Nike tongues tucked under laces,  
the bright swoosh whispering *run*  
though running is evidence, walking is evidence,  
breathing into a hood is breaking news.

Outside, suburbia rinses its teeth:  
cul-de-sacs white as communion wafers,  
SUVs asleep beneath basketball hoops,  
lawns clipped down to the grammar of obedience.  
A boy carries Skittles, small planets  
rattling in a pocket—red, yellow, green—  
a sugar galaxy Fox News will darken  
with a chyron, a photograph, the old machinery  
that turns childhood into probable cause.

Every window rehearses suspicion.  
Every porch light becomes an interrogation.  
Somewhere Tupac leaks from cheap earbuds,  
voice bruised gold, saying the rose, the concrete,  
the sirens already folding around the beat;  
somewhere a mother lowers the volume  
as if grief can be made less visible,  
as if bass itself might be accused  
of reaching for a weapon.

And there was Obama on the television,  
that immaculate seal, those flags  
standing upright as promises in a showroom,  
Hope printed cleanly enough for a tote bag,  
Change shining like a new appliance—  
while the drones of neighborhood watch  
circled the dark face in the gated dusk,  
while boys learned to sand down their names,  
empty their pockets, soften their shoulders,  
leave every gesture unopened.

At Target, under the red bull’s-eye,  
I practice disappearing:  
hands where the ceiling can see them,  
smile without teeth, voice without weather,  
no sudden reach toward the candy,  
no Tupac humming through the ribs,  
no anger bright as a sneaker box,  
no history dragging its chain of headlines.

I become beige carpet, coupon, cart wheel,  
the obedient ghost beside the fitting rooms;  
I fold myself smaller than a security mirror,  
smaller than the fine print beneath freedom,  
smaller than a Skittle melting  
its impossible rainbow into the tongue—

and still the lens follows,  
hungry, unblinking, American,  
still the screen fills with my outline,  
still someone asks what I was doing there,

as though I had not erased myself enough,  
as though erasure were not the oldest uniform,  
as though the body could survive  
by becoming less body, less night, less name,

until only the swoosh remains—  
white, swift, spotless—

running across the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
